/gifts.title: The Bread Baker's Gift Guide
/gifts.metaDescription: Handpicked tools, books and ingredients for people who bake bread. Sorted by category, by who you're shopping for, and by what you want to spend.
/gifts.intro: Every year people ask me what to buy the baker in their life, and every year I write this. Everything here is something I use, or something I'd hand a friend without hedging. Sorted three ways so you can find your way in: by what it does, by who it's for, or by what you want to spend.

topPicks.name: NutriMill Bosch Baker's Bundle
topPicks.pitch: If I were starting over, this is the machine I'd buy. It mixes stiff whole grain dough without straining, it mills your own flour, and it keeps up with a market table. Nothing else in this guide does all three.

topPicks.name: NutriMill Harvest Grain Mill
topPicks.pitch: Stone milled flour you cannot buy in any bag. Quiet enough to run in a shared kitchen, handsome enough to live on the counter. Fresh milled changes the first loaf, not the tenth.

topPicks.name: Goldie Starter Warmer
topPicks.pitch: Cold kitchens kill more starters than any other mistake. This holds the temperature for you, around the clock, and your feeding schedule finally behaves.

topPicks.name: Poco Lame
topPicks.pitch: The lame I hand to nervous new bakers. Small, forgiving, under twenty dollars, and it gets used every single bake.

/gifts/bake-day.title: Bake Day Gifts for Bread Bakers
/gifts/bake-day.metaDescription: Dutch ovens, baking steels, scales and the gear that shows up on bake day. Picked by a baker who uses them.
/gifts/bake-day.intro: Bake day is the part everybody pictures: the oven roaring, the dough going in, the crust cracking as it cools. This is the gear that decides how that goes. Heat, steam, and something to lift a hot loaf without leaving skin behind.

/gifts/proofing-temp.title: Proofing and Temperature Gifts for Bread Bakers
/gifts/proofing-temp.metaDescription: Proofers, bannetons, containers and thermometers. Temperature is the variable most home bakers never control, and it's the one that matters most.
/gifts/proofing-temp.intro: Temperature is the variable nobody tells you about, and it's the one running the whole show. A dough at 78 degrees and the same dough at 68 are two different recipes. These are the tools that let you stop guessing.

/gifts/scoring-shaping.title: Lames and Shaping Tools for Bread Bakers
/gifts/scoring-shaping.metaDescription: Lames, bench knives, whisks and mats. The tools you hold in your hands, from makers who care how they feel.
/gifts/scoring-shaping.intro: Scoring is where a loaf stops being dough and starts being yours. A good lame is not about the blade, it's about the handle and the balance and whether you trust it enough to commit to the cut. These are the ones worth holding.

/gifts/starter-care.title: Sourdough Starter Care Gifts
/gifts/starter-care.metaDescription: Warmers, jars, dehydrators and a dried starter that wakes up in a few days. Keep a starter alive through a cold kitchen.
/gifts/starter-care.intro: A starter is a pet that eats flour and forgives almost nothing about temperature. Most of what goes wrong in sourdough traces back to a starter that was too cold, too neglected, or too new. This is what keeps one healthy.

/gifts/milling-flour.title: Grain Mills and Flour for Home Bakers
/gifts/milling-flour.metaDescription: Grain mills, whole berries and specialty flours. Fresh milled flour tastes like something. Bagged flour tastes like the bag.
/gifts/milling-flour.intro: Flour goes flat. Not spoiled, just flat, and it happens faster than anyone tells you. Mill it yourself and the difference in the first loaf is not subtle. This is the equipment and the grain worth milling.

/gifts/books-learning.title: Bread Books and Baking Guides
/gifts/books-learning.metaDescription: Books on sourdough, bread history and selling what you bake. Including a free starter guide and a recipe collection.
/gifts/books-learning.intro: Tools only take you so far. At some point you want to know why the thing you did worked, so you can do it again on purpose. These are the books I wrote and the ones I keep going back to, plus two free things that cost nothing but a click.
/gifts/books-learning.pinnedPick: Sourdough for the Rest of Us

/gifts/wood-serving.title: Wooden Bowls, Boards and Serving Gifts
/gifts/wood-serving.metaDescription: Hand-turned bowls, bread boards and rolling pins. Pieces that mix the dough and then go on the table.
/gifts/wood-serving.intro: Wood keeps dough at room temperature when a metal bowl would chill it, and it looks like something on a table when the bread comes out. These are hand-turned pieces from a mill in Michigan. Buy one once and it outlasts you.

/gifts/storage-gifting.title: Bread Storage and Gift Wrapping for Homemade Loaves
/gifts/storage-gifting.metaDescription: Bread bags, slings and wraps. Keep a crust crisp for days, or give a loaf away in something better than a plastic sleeve.
/gifts/storage-gifting.intro: You spent eighteen hours on that loaf. Do not put it in a grocery bag. These keep a crust crisp past the first morning, and the holiday bags turn a gifted loaf into an actual present.

/gifts/new-bakers.title: Gifts for New Sourdough Bakers
/gifts/new-bakers.metaDescription: For someone who just started, or is about to. Nothing here assumes they already own a shelf of specialty gear.
/gifts/new-bakers.intro: Shopping for someone who just caught the bug. The trap is buying the thing an experienced baker would want, which usually sits in a drawer. Start with what gets used every single bake: something to mix with, something to score with, something to bake in.

/gifts/serious-bakers.title: Gifts for Serious Bread Bakers
/gifts/serious-bakers.metaDescription: For the baker who already owns the basics and wants the thing that actually changes the loaf.
/gifts/serious-bakers.intro: This one is harder, because they already own the obvious stuff. What they don't have is the thing that fixes a problem they've stopped complaining about: uneven heat, a dull blade, a proof they can't control. Buy the fix, not another gadget.

/gifts/market-sellers.title: Gifts for Bakers Who Sell What They Bake
/gifts/market-sellers.metaDescription: For the farmers market table and the cottage bakery. Volume gear, packaging, and the book on how to actually do it.
/gifts/market-sellers.intro: Selling bread is a different job from baking it. You need volume, consistency, packaging that survives a car ride, and a real understanding of what you're allowed to sell and for how much. This is the gear and the reading for that.

/gifts/under-25.title: Bread Baking Gifts Under $25
/gifts/under-25.metaDescription: Real tools under twenty-five dollars. Stocking stuffers that get used instead of drawered.
/gifts/under-25.intro: The best gift in this whole guide might be a fourteen dollar bench knife. Small tools get used every bake, which is more than you can say for most expensive ones. Nothing here is filler.

/gifts/25-75.title: Bread Baking Gifts $25 to $75
/gifts/25-75.metaDescription: The sweet spot. Serious tools at a price that doesn't require a conversation first.
/gifts/25-75.intro: This is where most of the good stuff lives. Enough money to buy something made properly, not so much that you need to check with anyone first. If you only look at one price band, make it this one.

/gifts/75-150.title: Bread Baking Gifts $75 to $150
/gifts/75-150.metaDescription: Gifts that solve a real problem: cold kitchens, weak oven spring, dull knives.
/gifts/75-150.intro: At this price you stop buying accessories and start buying solutions. A warmer that ends the cold kitchen problem. A steel that fixes a pale bottom crust. These are the ones that change how the bread comes out.

/gifts/splurge.title: Splurge Gifts for Bread Bakers
/gifts/splurge.metaDescription: Cast iron built for bread, grain mills, heirloom bowls and stand mixers that handle real dough.
/gifts/splurge.intro: The big ones. Everything here is something a baker would be thrilled to own and would never quite justify buying themselves, which is exactly what makes it a gift. Most of it will still be in the kitchen in twenty years.

/gifts/under-50.title: Bread Baking Gifts Under $50
/gifts/under-50.metaDescription: Real bread baking tools and books under fifty dollars. Lames, bannetons, scales, and starter kits worth giving.
/gifts/under-50.intro: Fifty dollars buys more in bread baking than it does in most hobbies. A lame that holds an edge, a banneton that actually shapes a loaf, a scale you'll still be using in ten years. Some of these also show up on the under twenty-five and twenty-five to seventy-five pages. That's on purpose, because fifty is the number people actually shop.
